notes.meaning: God did not literally forget Noah, because God never forgets any of His creatures. In Scripture, God remembering someone means He is turning His attention toward them to show mercy and act on their behalf. He sent a drying wind across the earth so the floodwaters would begin to go down.

God stopped the flood by shutting the underground water sources and stopping the torrential rain from heaven. The waters did not vanish all at once, but drained away slowly and steadily over one hundred and fifty days. The same God who sent the judgment was the only One who had the power to bring relief.

The ark finally came to rest on the mountains of Ararat after months of drifting. Noah did not steer the ark himself, but God's watchful care guided the vessel safely to solid ground. This gave Noah and his family a peaceful resting place after a long and frightening storm.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that Ararat refers to the ancient mountainous region of Urartu rather than a single specific mountain peak.

notes.meaning: The floodwaters kept sinking lower and lower for several more months. Finally, on the first day of the tenth month, the tops of the highest mountains appeared like little islands. Seeing dry ground gave Noah and his family proof that God was steadily restoring the earth.

Forty days after the mountain tops appeared, Noah opened the window of the ark and sent out a raven. The raven flew back and forth, feeding on floating carcasses and perching on the outside of the ark without coming back inside. Noah used this scavenger bird to check whether the land was beginning to dry up.

Noah next sent out a dove to see if the ground was clean and dry enough for other creatures. Unlike the raven, the dove found no clean place to land, so she returned to the ark. Noah reached out his hand and pulled her safely back inside to protect her.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Christian writers saw the dove as an image of the Holy Spirit and the ark as the Church, which welcomes the soul fleeing a sinful world.

notes.meaning: Noah waited another week and sent the dove out a second time. She returned in the evening carrying a freshly plucked olive leaf in her beak. Because olive trees grow in lower valleys, this proved that the waters had dropped far down and plant life was returning.

Noah waited another seven days before letting the dove fly out once more. This time she did not return, showing that she had found a dry, safe home in the open air. Noah's patient waiting from week to week shows how he trusted God's timing.

On New Year's Day, Noah peeled back part of the ark's roof and saw that the ground looked dry. Even though he could see the ground, he stayed inside for almost two more months until the soil was completely firm and ready for use. God knows the best time to end our waiting, even when we are eager to move forward.

God commanded Noah to leave the ark with his entire family and all the animals. God told the creatures to spread out and multiply, renewing the blessing of life that He had given at creation. Noah did not step out until God gave the command, showing faithful obedience.

Noah and his family left the ark just as the Lord had directed. Every animal, bird, and creeping creature followed them out in an orderly way, family by family. God had kept all of them safe through the entire year without losing a single soul.

Before building a home for himself, Noah first built an altar to worship God. He generously sacrificed some of the few clean animals and birds he had saved, offering them as a burnt offering to thank God for deliverance. True worship begins by honoring God first and giving Him our best.

God was pleased with Noah's heart of faith and worship, which pointed forward to the pleasing sacrifice of Jesus Christ. The Lord resolved never again to destroy all living creatures with a flood, showing mercy even though human hearts are naturally inclined to sin from their youth. God's grace leads Him to spare and protect us rather than give us what our sins deserve.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Douay-Rheims tradition translates this phrase as man being prone to evil, describing an inclination toward sin rather than declaring man's nature completely ruined.

notes.meaning: God promised that the natural cycles of planting, harvest, weather, and day and night will never fail as long as the earth exists. The flood had disrupted normal seasons, but God restored order to protect human life. This dependable rhythm reminds believers that God will always keep His promises.
